name: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
title: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
answer: Drafting proposals from past work covers the practice of turning completed research, publications, and project reports into new funding applications. It includes identifying reusable claims, methods, results, and impact statements from prior work and adapting them to a new call's requirements. The work sits within grant proposal development rather than scientific discovery itself, and it assumes an existing body of written research material. Professionals use it to reduce repetition and keep institutional memory consistent across applications.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting proposals from past work covers the practice of turning completed research, publications, and project reports into new funding applications. It includes identifying reusable claims, methods, results, and impact statements from prior work and adapting them to a new call's requirements. The work sits within grant proposal development rather than scientific discovery itself, and it assumes an existing body of written research material. Professionals use it to reduce repetition and keep institutional memory consistent across applications.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a document library of past proposals, papers, and reports, often stored as searchable text with metadata such as funder, year, and project status. Retrieval systems index this corpus so that relevant passages can be found by keyword, semantic similarity, or structured filters. Language models then operate on retrieved text, either in a local deployment or through an API, to generate draft sections. The infrastructure does not require training a new model; it typically uses retrieval augmented generation over an existing corpus.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common method is to extract claims and evidence from past work, then map them to the headings and evaluation criteria of the new call. The system retrieves candidate passages, checks them for fit against the funder's language, and rewrites them into proposal prose. Human reviewers edit the output to correct factual errors, remove outdated details, and align tone with the target funder. The process is iterative, with drafts compared against past successful and unsuccessful applications where available.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on provenance, plagiarism, and confidentiality. Draft text drawn from past work must be traceable to its source document so that reviewers can verify claims and avoid self-plagiarism across submissions. Systems should not reuse confidential reviewer comments or unpublished data without permission, and they must respect funder rules about simultaneous submission. Provenance records, such as source document identifiers and extraction timestamps, help maintain accountability when a proposal is audited.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward tighter integration with funding databases and institutional research information systems, so that past work is matched to calls automatically. Future tools are likely to include stronger claim verification against cited papers and automated checks for consistency between budgets, timelines, and narrative text. As language models improve at long document summarization, drafting may shift from sentence-level reuse to whole-section synthesis from multiple past projects. The main constraint remains the quality and organization of the underlying past work corpus.
